hook: The barefoot questioner of Athens, who chose death over silence.

pages.x: Socrates was born in Athens around 470 BC, the son of a stonemason and a midwife. He fought bravely as a foot soldier, walked barefoot even in winter and was famously ugly, with a snub nose and bulging eyes. He wrote nothing down; we know him through his pupils, above all Plato.
pages.cap: The Agora of Athens, where he talked with anyone who would listen

pages.x: A friend asked the oracle at Delphi whether anyone was wiser than Socrates. The answer was no. Puzzled, he went round questioning politicians, poets and craftsmen, and found they all believed they knew things they did not. He decided he was wiser only in knowing that he knew nothing.
Instead of lecturing, Socrates asked questions. What is justice? What is courage? Each answer led to another question, until the speaker saw the holes in his own ideas.
pages.fx: Testing ideas by questioning them is the heart of philosophy, science and the law. Teachers and law schools still call it the Socratic method.

pages.x: He called himself a gadfly, a stinging fly sent by the gods to keep the lazy horse of Athens awake. Young nobles loved watching him puncture important men. The comic poet Aristophanes mocked him in a play, The Clouds, where he dangles in a basket in the air to study the sky.

In 399 BC, after Athens had lost its war with Sparta, three citizens charged him with not honouring the gods of the city and corrupting the young. He refused to beg for mercy: "The unexamined life is not worth living." A jury of 501 citizens found him guilty and sentenced him to death.

His friends arranged an escape, but he would not break the law. He spent his last day discussing whether the soul lives on after death, then calmly drank a cup of poison hemlock. His last words reminded a friend to pay a debt: "We owe a rooster to Asclepius."
pages.cap: The Death of Socrates, by Jacques-Louis David

pages.x: Socrates turned philosophy from the stars to how we should live, and his habit of questioning everything is a root of Western thought. Through his pupil Plato and Plato's pupil Aristotle, he shaped 2,000 years of ideas.
pts: Taught by asking questions: the Socratic method
Chose death rather than give up his beliefs
